query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of Zr to HfMoTaTiZr will reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and elevated temperatures.
generation.conditions: room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 1000 °C)
generation.mechanism: The addition of Zr will lead to a reduction in density due to its lower atomic mass, while the solid solution strengthening effect will maintain the mechanical properties of the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: reduced density without sacrificing mechanical properties
generation.baseline: as-cast HfMoTaTiZr with a density of 10.21 g cm−3
generation.boundary: temperature range: room temperature to 1000 °C, loading conditions: compressive and tensile loading
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of density reduction and the effect of Zr addition on the mechanical properties at elevated temperatures are uncertain and require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare HfMoTaTiZr alloys with varying Zr content and measure their density and mechanical properties at room temperature and elevated temperatures.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Zr does not lead to a reduction in density or a significant degradation in mechanical properties at room temperature and elevated temperatures, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The NbTaHfTiZr HEA has received a lot of interests among all RHEAs, since it has a totally disordered BCC solid-solution structure with a melting point of about 1800 °C [,]. At normal temperature and cryogenic temperatures, the NbTaHfTiZr RHEA combines excellent strength and ductility []. The NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA based on this alloy not only maintains excellent room-temperature plasticity but also further improves its strength and has a good cold workability []. In order to explore the potential of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA for high-temperature applications, it is very necessary to study its mechanical properties at high temperatures. Here, we explore the mechanical properties of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy from RT to 1227 K and analyze its microscopic deformation mechanism. At the same time, we construct the constitutive equation of this alloy through a stress–strain curve in a deformation temperature range of 873–1173 K and a 0.001–0.1 s−1 strain-rate range and quantify the relationship between the strength and temperature.

The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo. Most medium entropy alloys (MEAs) exhibit excellent mechanical properties, but their applications are limited because of their high density. This study explores a series of lightweight nonequiatomic Ti65(AlCrNbV)35-xZrx (x = 3, 5, 7, and 10) MEAs with a low density, high strength, and high ductility. To achieve solid solution strengthening, Zr with a large atomic radius was used. In addition, various thermomechanical treatment parameters were adopted to further improve the MEAs’ mechanical properties. The density of the MEAs was revealed to be approximately 5 g/cm3, indicating that they were lightweight. Through an X-ray diffraction analysis, the MEAs were revealed to have a single body-centered cubic structure not only in the as-cast state but also after thermomechanical treatment. In terms of mechanical properties, all the as-cast MEAs with Zr additions achieved excellent performance (>1000 MPa tensile yield strength and 20% tensile ductility). In addition, hot rolling effectively eliminated the defects of the MEAs; under a given yield strength, hot-rolled MEAs exhibited superior ductility relative to non-hot-rolled MEAs. decision.trend: Research on high-entropy alloys (HEAs) has focused on improving their mechanical properties, such as strength and ductility, while reducing their density. Studies have explored the effects of different elements, such as Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr, on the properties of HEAs. The use of Zr has been shown to improve the mechanical properties of HEAs, including their strength and ductility. Additionally, thermomechanical treatment has been used to further improve the properties of HEAs.
decision.unsolved: The high density of HEAs, such as HfMoTaTiZr, remains a challenge. Reducing the density of HEAs without sacrificing their mechanical properties is a key goal of current research.
decision.why: The addition of Zr has been shown to improve the mechanical properties of HEAs, including their strength and ductility, while potentially reducing their density. This makes Zr addition a promising approach to reducing the density of HfMoTaTiZr without sacrificing its mechanical properties.
